hints: Focus on solubility differences, since filtering separates what dissolves in water from what stays solid.
Recall that $\text{BaSO}_4$ is famously insoluble while $\text{MgSO}_4$ is soluble, and $\text{BaO}$ forms soluble $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ in water.
Check which combination leaves an acid-resistant residue and also puts ions in the filtrate that form a white precipitate with sulfate.
walkthrough:
**Recall Group 2 solubility trends**

Think like a detective. Oxides react with water to make hydroxides. Solubility of hydroxides increases down the group, so $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is fairly soluble while $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is sparingly soluble.

For sulfates it is the opposite:
$$\text{MgSO}_4 \text{ soluble, } \text{BaSO}_4 \text{ insoluble}$$

**Interpret the solid residue test**

The residue does not react with $\text{HCl(aq)}$. A basic oxide like $\text{MgO}$ would dissolve and react:
$$\text{MgO(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow MgCl}_2\text{(aq) + H}_2\text{O(l)}$$ 
So the residue cannot be $\text{MgO}$. It must be an insoluble sulfate that resists dilute acid, which points to $\text{BaSO}_4$.

**Interpret the filtrate test**

The filtrate gives a white precipitate with $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(aq)}$. That means the filtrate must contain $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ ions:
$$\text{Ba}^{2+}\text{(aq) + SO}_4^{2-}\text{(aq) \rightarrow BaSO}_4\text{(s, white)}$$ 
$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ would not precipitate because $\text{MgSO}_4$ is soluble. So the soluble part must come from $\text{BaO}$:
$$\text{BaO(s) + H}_2\text{O(l) \rightarrow Ba(OH)}_2\text{(aq)}$$

**Put Q together**

We need an oxide that dissolves to give $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ in the filtrate, plus a sulfate that stays solid and resists acid. That is $\text{BaO}$ plus $\text{BaSO}_4$.

options.A: Correct. BaO reacts with water to form soluble Ba(OH)2 which passes into the filtrate. BaSO4 is insoluble so it stays as the residue and does not react with HCl. The filtrate contains Ba2+ which gives white BaSO4 precipitate with H2SO4. Both observations match perfectly.
options.B: Incorrect. Both BaO (as Ba(OH)2) and MgSO4 are soluble, but they would react together in water to precipitate BaSO4 immediately. With equal amounts, Ba2+ would be removed from solution, so the filtrate would contain mainly Mg2+ and would not give a white precipitate with H2SO4, since MgSO4 is soluble.
options.C: Incorrect. MgO is sparingly soluble and the unreacted MgO residue would react and dissolve in HCl to form MgCl2. Also the filtrate would contain very little Mg2+ and adding H2SO4 would give soluble MgSO4, so no white precipitate. Fails both tests.
options.D: Incorrect. MgSO4 dissolves to the filtrate but gives no precipitate with H2SO4. MgO remains largely as residue and would react with HCl. This is the opposite of the observations, which need an acid-resistant residue and a sulfate-precipitating filtrate.
